name: Olaus Magnus, Carta Marina et descriptio septentrionalium terrarum, Venice 1539
note: 13978x10394, uncoloured woodcut, the whole sheet. Olaus draws 'TILE' as a separate island south of 'ISLANDIA' and west of the Faroes ('FARE'), 778 x 571 px, crowded with towns and lettered 'Hec insula habet XXX millia popu[lorum] et amplius' and 'Hic habitat d[omi]n[u]s insulae', with a satellite islet off its west coast. Chosen by Etienne in October 2026, with the decision that Iceland stays: the Carta Marina is the depiction where Thule is not Iceland, so erasing Iceland as Californie erases California would contradict the source.
extraction_note: --mode band, density 0.4 over 15 px (0.3-0.4 is a plateau, 774-778 x 566-571 px; 0.45 leaks). Seed at (1316, 4732), the blank point of the west lobe farthest from any band pixel; the obvious seeds in the south fall on the band. A road drawn along the north shore (x 1415-1665, y ~4560) reads as band and walls off the strip of land north of it, so it is painted out (--blank-box 1415,4552,1665,4583), keeping clear of the coast; the strip and the north-west arm then join. The satellite islet off the west coast (58 x 56 px) is a pale core in the hatching and comes in with --islet 1282,4640 at an ink threshold of 130: at 110 a hair of paper between two hatch strokes joins it.
fit_note: NOT USED as a transform. A similarity fit on these four gives RMS 93 km, 0.21 km/px and a 47-degree rotation on a sheet that is north-up: Olaus draws the northern islands hugely oversized and crowded (Orkney ~5x, the Faroes ~2x, Shetland ~2-3x by extent), so spacing errors come out as a turn, as on Mercator's Tuscia. Tile projects to [-10.3, 59.2] under it. An exact affine on Islandia, Fare and Orcades puts it at [-12.2, 60.3]; on Islandia, Fare and Hetlandia at [1.2, 60.4] — Tile lies outside every triangle of real islands, so these are extrapolations and the last is nonsense. The two sensible readings agree on the area west of the Faroes and north of the Hebrides; [-11.0, 60.0] is placed between them.
